note_on_method: This is a state page, so most of it is a claim about coverage rather than about a court. Where it describes a place, the source is that operator's own publication — Seattle Parks and Recreation's GIS layer, the City of Bellevue's pages, the City of Vancouver's pickleball page, the City of Kirkland's court table, the City of Spokane's fields and sports page. Where it describes what is missing, it names the city we looked at and says why it is not here, because 'not listed' and 'does not exist' are different things and a reader deserves to know which one they are reading. This page exists because Bellevue was published on 4 September 2026, making Washington the second state with three verified cities. Spokane, the fifth city and the first east of the Cascades, was added on 7 September 2026 from a page that had to be read in a browser, because my.spokanecity.org refuses every scripted request. Nobody working on this has played on any court in Washington.

slots.coverage:
Washington has thirty-nine counties. This page covers five cities in three of them.

Forty-nine sites, 194 courts, five municipal operators of quite different kinds. King County holds forty of those sites and 144 of the courts: Seattle with twenty-four parks and 92 courts, Bellevue with thirteen venues and 42, and Kirkland with three and 10. Clark County holds three, all inside Vancouver, with 14 courts between them. Spokane County holds the other six, all inside the City of Spokane, with 36 courts - the first verified courts east of the Cascades in this state. Everything on this page is run by a city parks department. Not one private club, church gym, school or commercial facility appears, and that is a statement about what we have been able to verify rather than about where pickleball in Washington actually happens — our unverified import holds 653 rows across 169 Washington cities, and the great majority of the ones we have not checked are not municipal.

The four cities west of the Cascades arrived by four different routes, and the difference matters more than the total. Seattle publishes a dedicated pickleball dataset through its GIS portal, refreshed weekly, listing court counts, indoor/outdoor, lighting and nets per location — twenty-four venues confirmed from one authoritative file. Bellevue publishes no dataset at all, but it publishes one page stating a court count for every pickleball venue it runs, indoor and outdoor, each linked to a park page carrying the address. Vancouver publishes one pickleball page that states a count for three of the four venues on it. Kirkland publishes the clearest document of the four: a table whose column is headed "Number & Type of Courts", so each cell reads "6 pickleball courts" rather than a bare number that might be counting tennis courts - the only one of the four west-of-the-Cascades operators that removes that ambiguity in the heading itself; Spokane, further east, does the same with its two list headings.

Spokane's route was different again. The City publishes three lists on one page - tennis courts, tennis courts striped for pickleball, and dedicated pickleball courts - each line a park, a street address and a count, and the page cannot be fetched by a script at all: my.spokanecity.org answers every scripted request with a redirect into a "Checking Your Browser" interstitial. So the section was read in a browser on 7 September 2026, saved as text, and every line of all three lists is asserted against that file on every build. More than fifty other Washington cities in our import hold three or more rows that would clear the venue threshold on volume alone; not one of those rows carries a source, so none of them is published anywhere on this site.

What that leaves is a page that is honest about its shape: just under half the verified courts in Washington are in one city, forty of the forty-nine venues are in one county, and the state's second-largest city, Spokane, took until 7 September 2026 to appear at all - not for want of records but for want of access, on which see below.

The threshold that produces that shape is worth stating, because it is the reason this page is short rather than a judgement about Washington. A city appears here when three or more of its venues carry a source_url and a date_checked; a venue appears when an operator has stated its court count and an address that resolves. Nothing else qualifies a place — not the number of rows we hold for it, not how large the city is, not how obviously the courts exist. Two venues in this state clear everything except that bar and are named on their city pages rather than quietly dropped: Fisher Basin Community Park in Vancouver, for which the City states no court count and prints another park's address, and Sky Prairie Park in Spokane, for which the City states two courts and an address, "8501 N. Nettleton Ct.", that neither of this site's address resolvers finds at house-number level. A third, Highland Park in Bellevue, was in the same position until 4 September 2026, when this site added a second address resolver and its four courts became publishable - with the two other reservations about it carried onto its own page rather than dropped. All three are real places; only one of them is now a verified venue, and the difference between those two states is the whole point of the exercise.

What this page cannot tell you is how much of Washington's pickleball is municipal at all. Every venue here is city-run because city parks departments are the operators that publish; clubs, gyms, schools and commercial facilities generally do not, and the ones in our import arrived with no source attached. So read the coverage as a map of who writes things down, not a map of where the courts are.
slots.seasonality:
Washington is the state where the indoor question is not a preference, and the numbers here answer it badly.

Of 194 verified courts, 24 are indoor - roughly one in eight. All twenty-four are in Bellevue and Vancouver: fourteen across three Bellevue community centres and the Hidden Valley Fieldhouse, and ten in Vancouver's Firstenburg and Marshall community centres. Seattle, the city with just under half of the verified courts in the state and the wettest reputation in the country, has no verified indoor pickleball at all. Its parks dataset marks every one of its ninety-two courts outdoor. Indoor courts certainly exist in Seattle inside community centres and private clubs — several appear in our unverified import — but none has been checked against a named source, so none is listed. Spokane, east of the Cascades, is a blank on this question in the other direction: the City never writes "indoor" or "outdoor" against any of its thirty-six courts, so none of them is counted on either side of the line here.

The lighting picture is better recorded than in any other state we publish, because Seattle's dataset has a field for it. Five Seattle venues are lit: Bitter Lake Playfield, Rainier Beach Playfield, Miller Playfield, Alki Playground and Mt. Baker Park. Nineteen more are stated unlit, which is a different answer from unknown and is why those pages read No. Vancouver's Oakbrook Community Park is stated unlit too, in a sentence rather than a field: "The courts do not have lighting." Bellevue states nothing about lighting anywhere, so all thirteen of its venues read "not verified yet". Kirkland states nothing about lighting either, and adds a wrinkle of its own: all ten of its courts close at dusk, which settles the practical question without answering the recorded one. Spokane states nothing about lighting at any of its six parks, and no hours either, so its thirty-six courts carry no answer on either count. Put together: of forty-nine venues, five are known lit, twenty are known unlit and twenty-four are unknown - and in a state where it is dark by half past four in December, that first number is the one that decides whether an evening game is possible outdoors.

So the practical shape of a Washington winter, on what we can verify: five lit outdoor venues, all in Seattle, and twenty-four indoor courts, none of them in it.

The indoor courts come with conditions that a court count does not convey, and in this state they are the difference between a plan and a wasted drive. Every indoor venue in Washington that we have verified runs drop-in sessions on a published schedule, and not one of the six takes a booking. South Bellevue Community Center states it flatly — "All Drop-In Sports times are strictly drop-in only", with reservations, saved spots and signing in for another player all specifically disallowed — and asks you to check in at the front desk first. Crossroads Community Center says "No registration required: first-come, first-served. Space is limited." Vancouver's Firstenburg and Marshall centres run scheduled play for ages 12 and up. A gym is a pickleball venue only during the hours it is one, so the schedule matters more than the court count, and only one of these operators publishes a schedule we could read as anything other than a PDF dated two years ago.

Two further caveats belong to winter specifically. Bellevue's North Bellevue Community Center carries the only warning about a room rather than a court anywhere in this state — the City counts it as "2 courts (with low ceiling)" — and Vancouver's Firstenburg is the only indoor venue whose floor is on the record, a wood gymnasium floor rather than an unnamed hard surface. Everywhere else you are turning up to a surface nobody has described.
slots.notable:
The biggest verified site in Washington is in Spokane. Mission Park holds sixteen pickleball courts, striped on the park's eight tennis courts - two pickleball courts to a tennis court, shared with tennis - and the City states nothing else about it: no hours, no lighting, no surface, no price. Comstock Park, also in Spokane, is second at twelve courts on six. Then come four Seattle sites at exactly the same size: Bitter Lake Playfield, Green Lake Park's east courts, Rainier Beach Playfield and West Magnolia Playfield each hold eight courts. Two are lit and two are stated unlit, which between them is a fair summary of what Seattle Parks records: excellent coverage of the questions it chose to answer, and complete silence on cost and surface. Spokane's two large sites are the mirror image - a count and an address, and silence on everything else.

The largest indoor rooms are a tie at six courts — South Bellevue Community Center and Vancouver's Firstenburg Community Center — and they are worth reading beside each other, because they are the two venues in Washington that answer questions nobody else does. South Bellevue is the only venue in the state that publishes a price: $4 for Bellevue residents, $5 for everyone else, per adult drop-in session, with family sessions free for an adult and a child under 18 from the same household. It is also the only one that says who supplies the equipment — "We provide pickleball balls, nets, and poles". Firstenburg is the only venue in Washington with a verified playing surface of any kind, because Vancouver wrote down that its six courts are "on a wood gymnasium floor", and a gymnasium floor is a material rather than a category. Across the other forty-eight venues in this state, surface is unverified everywhere.

For dedicated courts — pickleball and nothing else, no tennis lines, no portable net — Washington has five places on the record. Peter Kirk Park in Kirkland has six, converted from tennis courts in 2026. Eastgate Park in Bellevue has four, permanently so since 1 September 2026. Oakbrook Community Park in Vancouver has four, open 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily with nets and poles permanently installed, which is as close to turn-up-and-play as this state gets outdoors. Corbin Park and Underhill Park in Spokane have two each, on the City's "Dedicated Pickleball Courts" list, with nothing stated about hours, nets or lights. Everything else verified in Washington is a shared court: tennis lines at thirty-odd venues, including thirty-two of Spokane's thirty-six courts, a basketball court at Bellevue's Lewis Creek Park, and a tennis net you play over at two more.

A few venues are notable for what they answer rather than for their size. Hidden Valley Park in Bellevue is one of only nine venues anywhere in this directory with a court count above zero on both sides of the indoor/outdoor line, and was the first: three courts in its fieldhouse and two in the park outside, at one address, listed by the City as two separate entries and published here as one place. Hillaire Park is the only venue in the state whose operator splits its own count by type — "3 courts (1 dedicated, 2 portable nets)" — so you know before you go which of the three is reliably pickleball. Lewis Creek Park is the only one in Washington whose pickleball shares with basketball rather than tennis, and the only one where a city has said what the overlay is drawn on. At the other end, Cherry Crest Mini Park has a single court over a tennis net, which is worth knowing precisely because "has pickleball" and "has a court free for you" are not the same sentence at a one-court venue.

The most useful sentence published by any Washington operator is not about a venue at all. It is Bellevue's: "Bellevue's pickleball courts are shared use with tennis courts, unless otherwise noted." A city that writes down its own default has told you what every unmarked entry on its list means, and it is the reason twelve Bellevue venues carry a sourced note about what kind of court you are walking onto while ninety-two courts in Seattle carry none.
slots.growth:
Two Washington cities converted tennis courts to dedicated pickleball courts in 2026, and between them they are the clearest evidence of what is happening to the sport in this state.

Kirkland did the larger one. The City closed the six tennis courts at Peter Kirk Park on 13 April 2026 "for conversion to six dedicated pickleball courts", and reopened them as pickleball courts on 2 July 2026 at 3 p.m. Six tennis courts in, six dedicated pickleball courts out, at the park next to the city's downtown - and it left a mark in our own data that is worth naming, because the imported dataset this site was built from has no row for Peter Kirk Park at all. The import was taken while it was still a tennis venue.

The second is six days old at the time of writing, and it is a City press release.

On 28 August 2026 Bellevue Parks & Community Services announced that, "responding to increasing community demand", it would convert the two dual-use outdoor sport courts at Eastgate Park into "a dedicated pickleball-only facility". From 1 September the tennis nets came off and the four pickleball courts marked on those courts became permanent, with a resurfacing to pickleball lines only planned to follow. The City cited "multiple recreation planning assessments and high interest in the sport expressed through community feedback", and named four nearby parks — Silver Leaf, Lakemont, Spiritridge and Sunset — where displaced tennis players could go, two of which are pickleball venues on this site.

The same notice contains the sentence that makes it useful rather than merely cheerful: the department "does not currently have conversions planned at any other dual-use courts in Bellevue". That is a stated negative, and it bounds the story. One park converted, none scheduled to follow, in a city with forty-two verified courts. Bellevue's restraint is its own; Kirkland's conversion two months earlier shows it is not the whole state's. Our build asserts that sentence is still present on the City's page, so if another conversion is announced this page fails rather than going on quietly claiming nothing is coming.

Against that, the shape of provision across the state has not moved. Most of what is verified in this state is still a shared court rather than a built one. Bellevue states the arrangement outright - shared use with tennis unless otherwise noted - and only five venues in Washington are dedicated pickleball on the record: Peter Kirk Park in Kirkland, Eastgate Park, Oakbrook Community Park, and Corbin Park and Underhill Park in Spokane, two courts each. That is what growth looks like almost everywhere before it looks like construction: lines painted on tennis courts, portable nets, and a dedicated facility every so often when a city decides the demand has settled. What we cannot tell you is whether this is representative, because five cities is five cities. Seattle's dataset is refreshed weekly by the city, so if its counts move we will see it; Bellevue's, Vancouver's and Spokane's are web pages that change without telling anyone, which is why all three are snapshotted and asserted on every build.

The other thing changing here is the record rather than the courts. Seattle's dataset is maintained as infrastructure — refreshed weekly, last edited on 31 August 2026 — which makes it the only Washington source that will tell us when a count moves. Bellevue's, Vancouver's and Spokane's are web pages maintained by people with other jobs, so all three are snapshotted into this repository and re-asserted on every build: if the City of Bellevue quietly edits the sentence stating that no further conversions are planned, or Vancouver fixes the address it prints twice, or Spokane renumbers a park, the build fails and someone reads the page again. That is the only defence a directory has against a fact that was true when it was written.

What would change this page most is not another conversion but another city, and the latest one shows what that takes. Spokane was, for three days, the most valuable page in Washington this project could not read: the City publishes a court count and a street address for every park with a court, and its site answers a plain request, a full browser header set and the web fetcher alike with a redirect into a "Checking Your Browser" interstitial. It was read in a browser on 7 September 2026 instead, saved as text and asserted line by line, which is how it came to be here. It also brought the state's clearest arithmetic on shared courts: the City's tennis list and its striped list together show two pickleball courts to a tennis court at Mission, Comstock and Peaceful Valley, and one to one at A.M. Cannon, so a reader knows how many slabs the count stands on. After Spokane the queue runs Redmond, Bellingham, Kent, Tacoma - cities where we hold enough rows to clear the venue threshold and no source to publish any of them. Redmond refuses us outright, as Kirkland did until it abruptly did not, and as Spokane did until it was read by hand. Each one is a parks department's web page away from being here, which is a small distance and, on the evidence of the cities published so far, a completely unpredictable one.

faqs.q: How many pickleball courts are there in Washington?
faqs.a: Nobody can tell you honestly, and this page will not pretend to. What we can tell you is what has been checked: 194 courts across forty-nine venues in five cities, each with a named source and a date. Our unverified import holds 653 rows across 169 Washington cities, which is a measure of how much is unchecked rather than a count of anything.

Because five is how many have a source we can show you. A city appears here once three or more of its venues carry a source_url and a date_checked. More than fifty other Washington cities in our import hold three or more rows that would clear the threshold on volume — Redmond, Bellingham, Kent, Tacoma, Marysville, Auburn, Kennewick, Olympia — and not one of those rows carries a source, so none of them is published.

faqs.q: How was Spokane checked, if its website blocks scripts?
faqs.a: By reading it in a browser. my.spokanecity.org answers every scripted request this project makes — a bare fetch, a full browser header set and the web fetcher — with a redirect into a "Checking Your Browser" interstitial, on 4 September 2026 and again on 7 September. The City's Recreational Fields and Sports page was opened in a browser on 7 September, its "Tennis and Pickleball Courts" section expanded, and the text saved with a header stating the method. Every line of its three lists is asserted against that file on every build, and the re-check is the same browser read repeated.

faqs.q: Where can I play indoors in Washington?
faqs.a: Bellevue and Vancouver, and nowhere else on this site. Fourteen indoor courts across South Bellevue Community Center (six), Crossroads Community Center (three), the Hidden Valley Fieldhouse (three) and North Bellevue Community Center (two, and the City warns of a low ceiling); ten more at Vancouver's Firstenburg Community Center (six, on a wood floor) and Marshall Community Center (four). All six are drop-in on published schedules and none can be booked. Seattle's dataset marks every one of its courts outdoor, Kirkland's courts close at dusk, and Spokane's City page never writes indoor or outdoor against any court at all.

faqs.q: Is it free to play in Washington?
faqs.a: Not verified anywhere in this state, and that is not the same as no. Three venues state that a fee applies — South Bellevue Community Center at $4 for residents and $5 for others, and Vancouver's Firstenburg and Marshall centres, which say a daily drop-in fee applies to non-members without publishing the amount. The other forty-six venues, including every park court in Seattle, Bellevue, Kirkland and Spokane, say nothing about cost at all. Spokane comes closest to a price without giving one: a court there can be officially reserved with a reservation permit by online form, and the City never says what the permit costs. They are municipal park courts and are very likely free; "very likely" is not a fact and does not go in a field.

Five, all in Seattle: Bitter Lake Playfield, Rainier Beach Playfield, Miller Playfield, Alki Playground and Mt. Baker Park. Nineteen more Seattle venues are stated unlit, and so is Oakbrook Community Park in Vancouver. Bellevue states nothing either way about any of its thirteen venues, and neither does Kirkland about its three or Spokane about its six, so those twenty-two, and two of Vancouver's three, read "not verified yet" — which means nobody has told us, not that the courts are dark.

faqs.q: What is the biggest pickleball site in the state?
faqs.a: Mission Park in Spokane, with sixteen pickleball courts striped on its eight tennis courts; Comstock Park, also in Spokane, is next at twelve on six. Both are shared with tennis, so the count you find depends on who is playing. West of the Cascades four Seattle parks tie at eight: Bitter Lake Playfield, Green Lake Park's east courts, Rainier Beach Playfield and West Magnolia Playfield. Indoors, South Bellevue Community Center and Vancouver's Firstenburg Community Center tie at six.

faqs.q: Can I book a court anywhere in Washington?
faqs.a: Only in Spokane, and only by permit. The City of Spokane writes that its tennis and pickleball courts are first-come-first-served, "however if you would like to officially reserve a court and receive a reservation permit please fill out the online form" — with no price, no lead time and no calendar published. Nowhere else: Bellevue's indoor sessions are explicitly drop-in only, with reservations and saved spots specifically disallowed at South Bellevue; its outdoor courts take no bookings; Vancouver states its courts "cannot be reserved" and are first come, first served with a paddle-rack rotation; Kirkland's courts are drop-in, open 8 a.m. to dusk; and Seattle Parks publishes no reservation system in the dataset we read.

faqs.q: How do you decide which Washington city to add next?
faqs.a: By whether its operator has written the courts down. Volume in our import is a tiebreak, not a qualification — the question is always whether a parks department publishes a court count we can quote, snapshot and re-check. Spokane was first in the queue on both counts and is now published, read by hand because its site refuses scripts. Redmond, Bellingham, Kent and Tacoma follow. A city with fifty rows and no municipal source stays unpublished behind a city with four rows and a page that states them.

faqs.q: What does "not verified yet" mean on these pages?
faqs.a: That the operator has not stated it, and that we refuse to guess. It is not a claim the thing is absent. Surface is unverified at forty-eight of Washington’s forty-nine venues; cost at forty-six; lighting at twenty-four. Those courts have surfaces, and most of the park ones are almost certainly free to play on. The moment a city writes either down, the field fills in and the source and date appear beside it — which is why the empty fields are left visible rather than hidden. A directory that quietly renders an unknown as a "no", or worse as a confident "free", is telling you something nobody told it.

Seattle’s dataset is refreshed weekly by the city and was last edited on 31 August 2026; we read it on 3 September. Bellevue and Kirkland were read on 4 September and Vancouver on 3 September, and all three are static web pages that change without notice, which is why each is snapshotted into the repository and re-asserted on every build. Spokane was read in a browser on 7 September, because its site refuses scripts, and its re-check is a person opening the page again and comparing it with the saved text. A re-check cadence per field — an address changes rarely, a drop-in fee often — is a decision this project has recorded as open rather than quietly assumed.

Our own triage of the imported dataset: 653 rows across 169 Washington cities, of which fifty-six clear the three-venue threshold on volume alone. Spokane holds thirty rows with twenty-eight passing every gate but provenance; Redmond twelve, Bellingham twelve, Kent nine, Marysville eight, Tacoma eight. Every one of those rows is status=pending because none carries a source_url or a date_checked. These are claims about our dataset, not about Washington.
